strengths: Well-motivated technical approach with hierarchically-designed attention mechanism specifically tailored for multi-subject video generation and identity preservation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple complementary metrics (FaceSim, NexusScore, NaturalScore, GimeScore) and systematic ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Strong empirical results showing consistent improvements across all metrics compared to state-of-the-art baselines (FaceSim: 58.12%, Text-Video Alignment: 49.55%, Total Score: 54.33%)
Valuable dataset contribution with careful curation pipeline combining OpenS2V-Nexus, synthetic data, and manual annotations for diverse multi-subject scenarios
Compelling visual results (Figure 4) demonstrating superior identity preservation and temporal consistency, especially in complex multi-subject scenes
Strong reproducibility commitment with detailed architecture specifications, implementation details in appendices, and promise to release code and pretrained models
Practical demonstration of controllable video editing applications, showing method versatility beyond generation
Clear technical presentation of hierarchical attention mechanism with three well-justified levels (intra-subject, inter-subject, multi-modal)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily an engineering contribution combining existing techniques (Rectified Flow, hierarchical attention, VLM guidance, Flow-GRPO online RL) without major fundamental advances
Critical missing computational analysis: no inference time, memory requirements, FLOPs, or efficiency comparison with baselines despite complex multi-component architecture

Evaluation lacks human judgment—no user studies validating perceptual quality, identity preservation, or temporal consistency; heavy reliance on automated metrics (NexusScore, GimeScore) without established community validation

Insufficient generalization analysis: no evaluation on unseen subjects, out-of-domain scenarios, varying video lengths, or semantically novel concepts; limited to 180 subject-text pairs for evaluation
Inadequate failure case analysis: no discussion of method limitations, struggles with >3 subjects, challenging subject types, or problematic scene compositions; cursory limitations section

Limited ablation depth: no justification for three-level attention hierarchy vs. alternatives, no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, no comparison with alternative RL approaches or simpler post-processing
Dataset scale underspecified: training dataset composition not clearly quantified; potential biases from OpenS2V-Nexus and synthetic data not discussed; unclear training-test overlap
Technical presentation gaps: architecture overview (Figure 2) overly complex; VLM integration during inference underspecified; loss weights not explicitly stated; RL training hyperparameters missing

Evaluation methodology concerns: metric combination weights in 'Total Score' not justified; impact of reference image construction strategy (Figure 9) only qualitative; no quantitative analysis of ablation gains
Baseline coverage gaps: some comparisons with 2024-2025 methods; proprietary systems (VIDU, Pika, Kling) mentioned but not compared; missing very recent multi-subject generation work from 2025

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing the practical challenge of preserving individual identities in multi-subject video generation while maintaining temporal consistency and quality
Thoughtfully designed hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism with three-stage design (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) effectively preventing identity leakage
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, extensive metrics, thorough ablations (Table 2), and human preference study (200 participants) confirming superiority
Substantial and consistent quantitative improvements: FaceSum 66.10% (vs 41-48%), NexusScore 45.1% (vs 39-48%), with gains across temporal consistency and visual quality
Significant dataset contribution with 218K+ masked subjects and sophisticated multi-stage curation pipeline combining OpenS2V-Nexus, synthetic generation, and human annotation
Excellent presentation with clear architectural diagrams, comprehensive appendices with implementation details (Tables S.4, S.6), and training dynamics visualization
Demonstrated practical applicability beyond generation, including zero-shot video editing capabilities (Fig. 6) showing method versatility
Clever integration of VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as semantic guide to control feature extraction and anchor generation process
weaknesses: Limited fundamental technical novelty: hierarchical attention is conceptually straightforward, VLM guidance extends prior work (Phantom), and online RL follows standard GRPO patterns from prior literature

Reproducibility challenges with complex data curation pipeline requiring cutting-edge external tools (Nano Banana, PyScene detection), in-context learning capabilities, and resource-intensive human annotation
Computational overhead of online RL phase inadequately addressed; inference time not reported; scalability with computational budget unclear
Face-specific evaluation dominance: FaceSum metric doesn't capture body/clothing consistency; multi-subject scenario details relegated to appendix; scalability with 4+ subjects unexplored

Reward design concerns: empirical weight choices (wfid=0.6, wqual=0.4) lack principled justification; ablation (Table S.7) shows conflicting metric improvements suggesting incomplete understanding of reward trade-offs
Missing justifications for design choices: why is Face-Sim appropriate for identity? Hierarchical attention configuration not ablated; online RL solution to circularity problem feels standard
Limited generalization analysis: method primarily evaluated on face-centric scenarios; full-body multi-subject performance unclear; no cross-domain or diverse demographic evaluation
Baseline comparison gaps: Phantom (2021) dated; proprietary model comparisons (VIDU, Pika, Kling) cannot be independently verified; external model dependencies (OpenV-L) could introduce bias

Technical presentation could be clearer: dense notation in Sections 3.2-3.3 lacks intuitive explanation; flow matching formulation (Eqs. 1-4) relationship unclear; some key results relegated to appendix

Incomplete failure analysis and limitations discussion: brief conclusion section; no systematic failure case exploration; potential for reward hacking or catastrophic forgetting in online RL not thoroughly analyzed
